articles.title: General Robotics, led by Microsoft vets, says its AI has cut robot setup from a month to hours
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A Redmond, Wash., robotics software startup founded by former Microsoft researchers says its platform can now handle much of the work of getting a robot up and running in a factory, warehouse or other industrial setting, a job that used to take a team of engineers.

General Robotics said Wednesday that advances in GRID, its robot intelligence platform, have cut the process of onboarding a new robot from about a month to as little as two hours. The company calls the approach “Auto Engineering,” with each onboarded robot and diagnosed failure feeding back into the system and speeding up the next deployment.

“Before this moment, it would take us a team of experts to go and execute on behalf of our customers,” said General Robotics CEO and co-founder Ashish Kapoor in an interview. “Clearly non-scalable, clearly very expensive, and clearly will take a long time.”
With Auto Engineering, he said, “we can magnify and accelerate each engineer’s capability.”

Founded in 2023, the company has grown to about 50 employees, primarily engineers. It has raised nearly $34 million, most recently in an April round led by Construct Capital, with participation from Khosla Ventures, Accenture Ventures, Nvidia and Valo Ventures. PitchBook put the size of the round at $25 million; the companies didn’t disclose terms at the time.
Kapoor said General Robotics has roughly a dozen customers — large enterprises across manufacturing, logistics, energy and defense — and revenue in the millions of dollars.
Customers include HTX , the science and technology agency of Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs, which Kapoor said has been working with General Robotics for about a year and a half.
The company’s platform works with robot types including industrial arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, wheeled robots and drones, according to the company.

General Robotics is operating in a competitive and well-funded sector. Physical Intelligence , which builds foundation models for robots, has raised more than $2 billion. Nvidia — an investor in General Robotics, and the maker of the Isaac Sim simulation software built into GRID — is developing its own robot models and deployment tools.
Robot makers build good hardware, Kapoor said, but often lack the expertise to put it to work in a specific setting like a shipping terminal. “That last layer is missing.”

Before co-founding the company, Kapoor spent 17 years at Microsoft, ultimately as general manager of its autonomous systems and robotics research group in Redmond, where he created the open-source drone simulator AirSim. General Robotics co-founders Sai Vemprala (CTO) and Shuhang Chen came from the same Microsoft team.

GeekWire covered the launch in 2023 , when it was Scaled Foundations and billed itself as “ChatGPT for robots.” It had five employees at the time, focused on aerial robotics and drones, with backing from Khosla and E14 Fund. It later renamed itself General Robotics.

articles.title: With a headcount topping 800, Helion opens Seattle office in pursuit of fusion energy
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Helion Energy , in its hard-charging pursuit of fusion energy, has opened an office in downtown Seattle as its headcount swells to 800 employees.

The company already occupies five buildings in Everett, Wash., where it’s headquartered, plus operations in the central Washington town of Malaga, where Helion is building what it hopes could be the world’s first commercial fusion plant.
“Who would have thought it when we founded the company in 2013 with only five of us,” said CEO and co-founder David Kirtley in a GeekWire interview, marveling at the growth.
In June, Helion announced $465 million in new funding, bringing its total capital raised to more than $1.5 billion and its valuation to 10 times that figure.

The company is racing to master fusion, which produces energy by smashing together light atoms — essentially replicating the process that powers the sun and stars. No one has been able to create a commercially viable amount of energy from fusion here on Earth, though notable progress is being made by research institutions and private companies.
The planet is increasingly hungry for abundant, clean power as data centers gobble energy and transportation, buildings and industrial processes shift toward electrification.

That has helped spike interest in fusion, and the sector globally has raised $14.24 billion since 2021, according to the Fusion Industry Association, with multiple companies predicting they’ll succeed in producing sufficient energy in the next five to 10 years. Helion has one of the most ambitious targets, aiming to reach that mark in two years.
The company is No. 1 on the GeekWire 200 , a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

The company’s Seattle office is 15,631 square feet in the 8th + Olive building, in a space formerly occupied by Airbnb. The move comes as Seattle pushes to bring businesses back into its core: The city’s urban neighborhoods had an office vacancy rate of 28.2% in the second quarter of this year, with downtown alone at 34.9%, according to Kidder Mathews research .
Kirtley said they’re hiring and the goal is to have 100 employees downtown working on business and operations, recruiting and finance.

Back in Everett, teams are running tests on the company’s prototype fusion device, named Polaris, and working to get a smaller fusion machine called Tiny Merge online. The startup is also ramping up a facility for assembly work where employees and automated systems will manufacture energy-carrying capacitors, semiconductor modules and other hardware. The facility is currently producing initial test pieces.

The Malaga site will be home to the Orion facility and will include three buildings: an office building, already complete and in use; a building for final assembly of components shipped from Everett, also finished; and the generator building, which will house the 50-megawatt Orion generator and associated power electronics. So far the beams are up for the last building, with the goal of getting it “weather tight” before winter, Kirtley said.
Helion is charging ahead with Orion and building its manufacturing capabilities while continuing to tackle the physics challenges of producing energy from fusion.
The plant must be operational in two years to meet Helion’s contract with Microsoft to provide energy for a nearby data center.

articles.title: Race the Gr8
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: After a disastrous race last year , Route 8 called for a rematch. Since then, Mayor Wilson issued an executive order to build bus lanes on Denny Way, SDOT designed an eastbound bus lane , and the bus lane was installed . This year, Route 8 actually stood a chance.
The race kicked off at Denny Way & Dexter Ave at 5:41pm as bus 8266 crossed Dexter Ave.
The bus immediately left almost everyone in the dust. After the first block, only a few runners kept up with the bus.

The bus picked up dozens of riders at the stops near Westlake Ave and Fairview Ave before barrelling towards the finish line, behind just three runners. Bus 8266 finished at 5:45pm, clocking in a total race time of 4 minutes for the half-mile race. Last year, the bus took 21 minutes.
Congratulations to the three runners who beat the bus, the Fix the L8 campaign, and to everyone who advocates for improving transit service.

articles.title: Capitol Hill’s Hudson House apartments to become CoLEAD supportive housing on Summit Ave
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Capitol Hill’s Hudson House apartments, long operating as single-room occupancy rentals, is entering a new chapter under a supportive services partnership with Purpose. Dignity. Action., according to filings with the city.

Located at 1712 Summit Ave, the 1906-era 61-unit building has been serving as studio micro-apartments since its $4.5 million acquisition by the The Easton Group from Pioneer Human Services in 2024. Rents hovered around $799 a month, plus utilities.

Under its new plan, the building is being utilized as supportive shelter. On-site staff provide will provide intensive harm-reduction case management, room support, and exit coordination to guide residents off the streets and into housing, according to a recent job listing .

PDA, formerly known as the Public Defender Association, is a Seattle-based nonprofit dedicated to creating non-punitive, community-based alternatives to traditional criminal legal responses. Rather than developing or owning real estate, PDA focuses on diversion services, systems reform, and care coordination.
Ripples of the city’s increased spending on supportive housing and transition from eras of halfway houses and transitional apartments continue to be felt on Capitol Hill.

The largest project is planned for the 1700 block of Belmont Ave where the Downtown Emergency Service Center plans to eventually develop the parcels into a 120-unit permanent supportive housing facility. In the meantime, the land is being used to host Belmont Village , the neighborhood’s 31-tiny house village homeless shelter managed by the Low Income Housing Institute .
Capitol Hill’s Sharyn Grayson House, part of the county’s Health Through Housing program, is another example of recent supportive housing projects growing in the area.

The city and Mayor Katie Wilson continue to boost the approach. Kelli Larsen , the mayor’s new director of the Seattle Office of Housing played a key role in reauthorizing the Seattle Housing Levy and launching new funding initiatives via the JumpStart payroll tax for permanent supportive housing. The Office of Housing committed $27 million to Permanent Supportive Housing workforce wages at partners and contractors in its latest budget. Larsen, by the way, will appear in front of the Seattle City Council’s Housing, Arts, and Civil Rights Committee Wednesday afternoon as part of her confirmation process.

Across Seattle, PDA is best known for administering LEAD (Let Everyone Advance with Dignity) and its pandemic-era expansion, CoLEAD . Operating across a small, rotating footprint of leased hotels and residential buildings, the organization has paired low-barrier shelter with behavioral health and legal navigation. Through its model, PDA has helped unsheltered individuals find housing stability without relying on prosecution or detention.
In Pioneer Square, PDA is coming off a successful push this summer to move people off the streets in the lead-up to the city’s World Cup matches. Officials say the push exceeded goals .

Hudson House will be integrated into PDA’s efforts as CoLEAD lodging including “work with Participants to reduce illicit activity that has a community impact” and “coordinating communal activities to cultivate a sense of belonging and encourage constructive social interaction between participants.”

According to PDA, the CoLEAD Lodging Agreement establishes terms for occupancy without requiring sobriety or criminal background checks. Residents agree to avoid violence, weapons, open flames, drug sales, and substance use in shared hallways. Rooms are subject to routine safety checks, and guest visits are restricted. Participants commit to meeting with case managers while staff use de-escalation and mediation rather than immediate eviction when conflicts or rule violations occur.

articles.title: Seattle City Council takes up bill to protect consensual non-monogamy and diverse relationship structures
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: A proposal would extend civil rights protections in Seattle in areas such as housing and employment to individuals who are pansexual, asexual, or in consensual non-monogamous relationships, while also extending protections to those in multigenerational households.

The Seattle City Council’s Housing, Arts, and Civil Rights Committee meets Wednesday afternoon to consider the bill from Alexis Mercedes Rinck proposed to expand civil rights protections to cover diverse sexual orientations and relationship structures.

The measure would amend the Seattle Municipal Code by updating the definition of “sexual orientation” to include pansexuality and asexuality. It also removes gender-binary phrasing and establishes that protected practices include consensual relationships involving multiple partners, including non-monogamous relationships.
The protections apply to employment, housing, public accommodations, business licensing, park access, and policing policies enforced by the Seattle Office for Civil Rights .

Employers would not have to expand benefits. Rinck’s proposal establishes that non-monogamous relationships are protected expressions of sexual orientation rather than a distinct class, excluding any requirement for employers to provide health insurance, leave, or other compensation perks to multiple partners.
The legislation also addresses the existing “marital status” class, specifying that definitions of cohabitation would include multigenerational families living together.

Seattle is following cities like Portland and Olympia in adopting expanded protections against discrimination in housing, hiring, workplaces, public businesses, city parks, and policing. Under the bill, residents facing unfair treatment could file complaints and seek remedies through the Seattle Office for Civil Rights.
Under the proposal, the new policy is scheduled to take effect in mid-2027.

While the Office for Civil Rights can absorb initial administrative enforcement within its existing budget, department officials have requested up to $121,000 in supplemental funding during the 2027 budget process to finance community outreach and education.

paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week, I’ll catch up on some news that transpired while I was on vacation for the last three weeks. (I’m so glad nothing major happened, like the passing of Dolly Parton or the arrest of Tupac’s killer.) Miley Cyrus—now rebranding as just Miley—wants the kids back on the dance floor with her new single “Bass Persuades.” Plus, I’ll explain why this is a Macklemore stan column now.

This week in Strangerland , our September print issue hit the stands , which means there is a new calendar of music events that’ll keep you busy all month long. I also profiled the Music Genius Award winner Kay Redden (founder of Den Tapes). Plus, check out the profiles on fellow winners for food , performance , film , literature , and visual art categories, along with the shortlists . This is a Macklemore stan column now. During his opening set for Ed Sheeran in New Jersey on Friday, the Seattle rapper gave a version of a speech he’s given previously, advocating for the end of Israel’s genocide in Gaza. He stated: “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace. Love. For all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality. So I say free Palestine. I say free Lebanon. I say free Cuba. I say free Congo, free Sudan, free all people in America living in fear over this terrorist organization ICE. None of us will be free until we are all free.”

In response to the speech, the Israeli American Council released a petition calling on Sheeran to drop Macklemore from his tour. Macklemore has since shared the speech in full, captioning it: “Wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial.”

P!nk has also entered the Zionist group chat , sharing an Instagram post stating that claims of genocide are “false” and concertgoers are owed refunds. She then posted a series of memes that you might find your Republican aunt sharing on Facebook.

She’s just being Miley. Last week, the artist formerly known as Miley Cyrus announced that, in the legacy of single-named pop divas, she’s dropping her last name for her upcoming album, Bass Persuades . She dropped the album’s title track, which is in good company with modern dancefloor classics such as Beyoncé’s “Break My Soul,” Madonna’s “I Feel So Free,” and Lady Gaga’s “Abracadabra.” She even serves a “Vogue”-style rap, calling out zoomers who are too busy on their phones to go out and dance: “Glued your eyes to the telephone screen / But you missed the hit without MTV / Go analog (Yeah), make it cinema (Yeah) / Just look out the window and what do you see?”

articles.title: What Does the “Mamdani Moment” Look Like in Seattle?
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: Seattle’s media and political classes have inundated readers for months now with dubious stories about what the election of socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and a slate of aligned New York legislators means for left-wing politics in Seattle.

What none of these analyses have done is talk to the local affiliate of the nationwide socialist organization Mamdani and his slate are members of and owe their victory to, the Democratic Socialists of America. In the journalistic tradition of gathering information from people who know what they’re talking about, The Stranger sat down with the cochairs of Seattle DSA’s Electoral Working Group, who coordinate the organization’s efforts to win on the ballot.

What’s been the immediate effect of the Mamdani media circus on the organization? For starters, a large bump in membership over the past three months, says cochair Carlos Jimenez Guiza, from 2,000 to roughly 2,500.
“So we’re looking at like a 25 percent increase, which I think has been like the fastest spurt I’ve seen in the two years I’ve been here,” he says.

Jimenez Guiza is fairly new to DSA, first getting involved during Rep. Shaun Scott’s successful 2024 legislative campaign while living in Capitol Hill. Scott was the first DSA member elected to the Washington State Legislature. “Starting to organize to elect my own representative seemed like a kind of an organic way to get started,” Jimenez Guiza says.

While Seattle DSA has a number of working groups and committees devoted to socialist organizing across the community—from labor to Palestinian solidarity—most Americans experience politics through the lens of elections, and Jimenez Guiza credits electoral work as a specific tactic to attract and mobilize new members.
“It’s just like the lowest hanging fruit to engage with people about politics and changing the world,” he says.

Livey Beha, the Electoral Working Group’s other cochair, joined Silicon Valley DSA in 2019 and has been with the Seattle branch since 2022. She says that for people not paying attention to DSA, it may seem like the party’s big wins in New York came out of nowhere, when they were actually the result of years of electoral organizing and gradual victories. Seattle DSA wants to mimic that strategy and duplicate its success.

“We literally have a document that we reference as we train up our volunteers, from New York City, about their strategy, and it was written eight years ago, and we still reference that as like this is what they’re doing, and we’re trying to replicate, and we recognize we’re a few years behind,” she says.
In general, the idea is to devote member resources to a smaller number of winnable elections and use those victories to attract new members.

When that document was written, Mamdani was just another new DSA member working on unsuccessful election campaigns. But within a few years, he was one of nine DSA-endorsed candidates elected to New York’s state legislature. After helping Mamdani get reelected to his seat twice, NYC-DSA made a bid for the mayor’s office, and voters elected Mamdani in 2025, making him a household name.

Beha says that some of the group’s electoral strategy was “xeroxed over from New York to a certain extent” and helped them be strategic in how they approach races and choose candidates. “We’re not trying to win just one election. We’re trying to build a political machine,” she says.

After a long losing streak stretching back to the organization’s rekindling after Donald Trump’s election in 2016 (they had roughly 50 members at the time), Seattle DSA is going into the general election with two sure-thing legislative campaigns, doubling the number of socialists in the legislature within two years of electing their first representative.

Some of its success stems from the organization voting to amend their endorsement policy in early 2024 to focus solely on materially supporting candidates willing to get with DSA’s program and eschewing endorsements signalling general support to left-wing candidates outside the organization. A DSA endorsement isn’t just a sticker for a campaign flyer anymore. It is a commitment to join the organization and be accountable to its members in exchange for an army of organized campaigners. Even if for practical purposes trial and error has shown it’s critical to still run on the Democratic Party ticket, to construct a political machine, one must act like a party.

“We still want to run principled socialist campaigns, but we’re going to do what we can to make sure that they win, because that’s what actually drives growth. And I think those are just aspects of what’s kind of been emerging as a basic electoral strategy, diffusing initially from New York,” Jimenez Guiza says.

After years of losing elections, Seattle DSA won its first major victory in 2024, successfully mobilizing canvassers to first place a minimum wage increase on the ballot in Renton, and then getting voters to pass it.
“With Raise the Wage Renton, that was really our first big independent win, independent of too much outside support,” Beha says.

She says the first thing organizers have to do well is talk to voters—”Do you think the minimum wage should be higher? Why is it $4 less in Renton than it is in Seattle?”—and that the extended canvassing campaign in Renton informed their strategic door-knocking efforts and contributed to Shaun Scott’s subsequent win in the 43rd District.

What does this new endorsement process look like in practice? A recent example can be found in Seattle DSA’s vote to endorse Jaelynn Scott for the 37th Legislative District in the Washington House of Representatives this year, but not Katie Wilson for mayor last year.

The organization’s endorsement process is quite transparent. First, candidates fill out a detailed questionnaire. Then the Electoral Working Group questions them and offers a recommendation to members, and those members hold a Q&A with the candidates before a member-wide vote. Records of the process are posted online.
Jaelynn Scott was willing to go along with DSA’s requirements, she got the nod from the Electoral Working Group, and members voted to endorse her.

Katie Wilson’s application for an endorsement went quite opposite. According to Seattle DSA’s public records, Wilson wouldn’t commit to a number of key expectations of a DSA-endorsed candidate: She wouldn’t join DSA, identify publicly as a socialist in campaign materials, cross-endorse other DSA candidates, share election data such as volunteer lists and voter databases with the chapter, or commit to meeting with the Socialists in Office Committee that keeps DSA-endorsed candidates accountable to the organization (as Rep. Shaun Scott does on a regular basis).
Wilson’s policies on homeless sweeps, police funding, and Palestine were also out of alignment with the organization, according to the EWG Steering Committee’s recommendation not to endorse.

A resolution by elected chapter leaders recommending Seattle DSA not endorse Wilson also mentioned that the Transit Riders Union—cofounded and led at the time by Wilson—“sent an email encouraging its members to join Seattle DSA for the purpose of supporting Katie Wilson’s endorsement” (they weren’t thrilled by this).

In the chapter-wide vote, members chose not to endorse Wilson, though Seattle DSA still encouraged members to vote for her, and many members volunteered for her campaign. Come the general election, Wilson barely squeaked by with a 2,011-vote margin. Seattle DSA has since published a number of communiqués criticizing her sweeps of the homeless and flip-flopping on surveillance cameras. As for the independent socialist mayor’s stab at political endorsements (which many commentators compared to Mamdani’s), both her candidates lost badly in the primary election, while Seattle DSA’s won easily.

Despite years of support during elections from DSA, Seattle’s longtime socialist city council member Kshama Sawant also did not receive an endorsement from Seattle DSA for her congressional campaign, which did not survive the primary.
“Sawant was very clear that she was not interested in that type of endorsement,” Beha says.

A more recent application for endorsement was filed by 37th Legislative District candidate Kelabe Tewolde, a young progressive who beat long-term incumbent Democrat Rep. Sharon Tomiko Santos in the August primary.

Seattle DSA had scheduled endorsement Q&A meetings with Tewolde in late August, but he rescinded the application before they were held. Considering he’s in a good position to win the general election based on his primary performance, it could have been a good get for DSA to secure a third state legislator. (The group will be door-knocking in the 37th District for Jaelynn Scott anyway.)

“Shortly before he withdrew, he told us it was not the right time, and that he hopes to work with us in the future. We’re not really sure of the exact reason beyond that, so we don’t really want to speculate,” Jimenez Guiza says. “But just speaking for me, I hope that he just continues to engage with the organization in a way that hopefully in the future both he and our members think an endorsement is the right move.”
Asked by The Stranger why he rescinded his DSA endorsement application, Tewolde did not offer a direct reason.

“It’s exciting to see a generation of young, progressive leaders win primaries, and elected office nationwide. I’m inspired by these diverse voices, and the diverse viewpoints they bring to urgent policy and political discussions. Some of these leaders seek formal DSA support, and some do not. My campaign is building a broad-based coalition that is growing every day. I welcome support from all who want to be part of our growing movement for change, and I appreciate the support from DSA and others in this effort!” Tewolde wrote in an email.

So if Shaun Scott and Jaelynn Scott are both shoe-ins, and they’re not mobilizing to support Tewolde, what is Seattle DSA’s army of door-knockers going to do ahead of the November general election? While there will still be a field campaign for Jaelynn, members also voted to oppose hedge fund manager Brian Heywood’s right-wing ballot initiatives, so Seattle DSA members will be out fighting to preserve the Millionaires Tax and defeat the anti-trans agenda alongside the establishment left. All of it is useful experience building capacity for bigger campaigns down the line and creating a base of DSA-friendly voters in the 37th Legislative District, Jimenez Guiza says.
Seattle DSA is also planning to run a city council candidate during next year’s election—the first with ranked-choice voting—though there’s been no endorsement yet.

“I think the thing that gets me every time I just think about our work together is that it’s all volunteer,” Beha says. “Like, we are just normal people, like bartenders, bus drivers, office workers, who are just spending our evenings doing this together, and we’re up against folks who are professional politicals or the political class, and that we have seen some wins. To me, that is pretty astonishing.”

articles.title: A journalist coined ‘the Bible Belt’ 100 years ago – it’s been oversimplifying the South ever since
articles.author:
<name>John Hayes, Associate Professor of History, Augusta University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/john-hayes-2571766"/>
paras: “Look No Further!” a billboard on the side of the highway beckons, drawing my gaze toward the red cover of a Bible. “You Are Worthy of Redemption!”
Not far away, another sign urges me to “Keep Christ in Christmas.” Then farther down the road a third appears: “Jesus: COMING SOON” its bright colors announce.

Signs like these are familiar to me: I’m a historian who studies the U.S. South and lives in it. I know how easily they can evoke the South – or, I should say, a certain image of it. As that image pictures it, the South is “the Bible Belt”: a place where people are really religious, and, as a result, socially and politically conservative. Indeed, in this year of midterm elections, you’re almost certain to hear pundits invoke “the Bible Belt” as shorthand explanation for Southern political behavior.

The phrase has been around for a century . Its endurance, however – and the “evidence” behind it today – could use some serious scrutiny. I spotted those roadside signs, for example, in Ontario, Canada, a thousand miles from what anybody would think of as the South.
Of the many things said about the South over the years, “Bible Belt” is the cliché that just won’t die.

“Bible Belt” entered the lexicon in 1924, in the pages of The American Mercury , a magazine co-founded by H.L. Mencken. Based in Baltimore, at the upper edge of the South, Mencken was one of the nation’s most prominent journalists in the decades between the world wars.

The acerbic satirist had skewered the South in his much-discussed 1919 essay “ The Sahara of the Bozart ,” depicting it as a vast cultural wasteland. In 1925, he closely covered the Dayton, Tennessee, trial of biology teacher John T. Scopes, who had been charged with violating the state’s law against teaching Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution . Mencken famously lampooned it as the Scopes “monkey trial .”

He coined “Bible Belt” in his regular column of short news items, then employed the phrase routinely. By it he meant a place where two Protestant groups, the Baptists and the Methodists, dominated not just religious life , but also the mores of the whole society. The whole region, Mencken argued, was a Baptist-Methodist stranglehold where fun and free thought were banished.

It’s true that in the early 20th century, Baptists and Methodists dominated the South in a way that they didn’t anywhere else . To trace the bloc of states where over 50% of religious congregation members were Baptist or Methodist was to trace the region’s boundaries with uncanny precision.

But beneath commonalities, religious life was divided by both race and class. Black Baptists and Methodists met in their own churches: autonomous institutions that came to be known, collectively, as “ the Black church .” The region’s poor Christians drew on inherited traditions and their own hardships to craft a folk version of Baptist-Methodist faith – what I’ve written about as “hard, hard religion.”

These religious divisions paralleled political ones. Through techniques like poll taxes and literacy tests, Southern states severely restricted the franchise, effectively stripping Black and poor white Southerners of their voting rights.
The social order that Mencken described as the Bible Belt, then, expressed the culture of elite and middle-class white people, the ones with the political power to enforce it.

“Bible Belt” joined other phrases that expressed how the early 20th-century South differed from national patterns. Amid industrializing, urbanizing America, the South was “the Cotton Belt,” the world’s leading cotton producer, with a predominantly rural, agricultural population. Political contests marked the nation, but in the “Solid South,” the Democratic Party monopolized politics . With high poverty, low wages and limited capital, the South was the prosperous nation’s “ No. 1 economic problem ,” as President Franklin Roosevelt put it in 1938. And the violent racial oppression of the “Jim Crow South” was what many Black Southerners eagerly fled when doors of opportunity opened in other regions.

Most Southerners, like most Americans, live in suburbs and work in a service economy . Republicans hold a political majority in the region , but they have to compete for it. Southern-based corporations like Walmart, McKesson and Exxon Mobil are in the top 10 of the Fortune 500 . And what legal scholar Michelle Alexander calls “ the New Jim Crow ” – the system of mass incarceration that disproportionately criminalizes people of color – is not confined to the South, but nationwide.
Old lines of difference between the South and the rest of the nation have faded. So have the once-common nicknames that described them – with the stubborn exception of “Bible Belt.”

A quick glance at the news shows its persistence, with headlines discussing “ The Bible Belt’s Beliefs About Women ,” or describing one Arkansas town as “ the Bible Belt’s LGBTQ Oasis .” The cultural issues reported in stories like these are no doubt real, but framing them as expressions of an enduring Southern Bible Belt seems to imagine religion as unchanging, timeless.

In reality, both the region’s people and their religion are changing dramatically. More Black, Latino and biracial people live in the South than in any other part of the country. White people make up just 52.5% of the regional population . The rapidly changing South is dynamic, second only to the West in demographic diversity.

This shapes religion, too. As the 2023-2024 Pew Religious Landscape Study showed, Black and Latino Americans are more likely than white Americans to identify as Christian. The faith of Black Southerners (predominantly Baptist) and Latino Southerners (predominantly Catholic) is a reminder that the South is not a religious monolith.

Meanwhile, white Baptists and Methodists are not the force they used to be. Their main institutions, the Southern Baptist Convention and the United Methodist Church, have been declining in membership for decades . The same Pew study showed that a mere 12% of Southerners identify with either denomination .

Internally, both denominations have had major splits on whether women can be leaders and whether to recognize LGBTQ identities . Such splits reflect divides that sociologist James Davison Hunter diagnosed in 1991 as “ Culture Wars .”

Consider his book’s subtitle, though: “The Struggle to Define America.” In these culture wars, the battlefield is the nation. The fighters are not regions, but political factions. What they’re fighting over is the legacy of the social movements of the 1960s : civil rights, women’s rights, gay rights, the environment.

The fact that the culture wars for America can be found in the contemporary South is a testament to just how much the once-distinct region participates in the dynamics of national life. Those wars may sound louder in the South than elsewhere, but that’s not the expression of a changeless Bible Belt; rather, it is the historical pattern that reactions are often strongest where change is most pronounced.

articles.title: Pennsylvania is suing TikTok over ‘addictive’ features – but that’s messier than it sounds
articles.author:
<name>Jonathan Caulkins, Professor of Public Policy, Carnegie Mellon University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jonathan-caulkins-2718074"/>
paras: Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday announced a civil lawsuit against TikTok on Aug. 11, 2026, filed in Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas and accusing the social media platform of violating state consumer protection laws in ways that harm youth.
One is deceit: for example, making false statements about how much of TikTok’s content contains mature themes, and about the ability of its guardrails to protect youth from that content.

The second alleges that “TikTok knowingly created platform features intended to cause excessive, compulsive, and addictive use, despite knowing that young people are more susceptible to – and acutely harmed by – those features.” Those features include infinite scrolling, autoplay and push notifications designed to trigger the release of dopamine, the neurotransmitter that drives the brain’s reward system.

The company rejects the charges. In a statement to the Pennsylvania Capital-Star , a spokesperson for TikTok said, “This lawsuit relies on misleading and inaccurate claims and deliberately ignores the concrete safety measures TikTok has voluntarily implemented to support the well-being of our community.”

I’m a public policy professor, not a lawyer, so I won’t predict who’ll win in court. But after nearly 40 years studying how addictive products are marketed , I agree that goods and services that lead to compulsive behaviors – whether scrolling or smoking – deserve special scrutiny. However, they do not fall neatly into binaries such as being addictive or not, or dangerous for youth but safe for adults. Lawsuits that find defendants liable or not liable risk imposing black-and-white distinctions on trade-offs that require nuanced thinking.
There is a long history of binary thinking about addictive goods.
Drugs such as heroin were seen as dangerous and bad, so they were banned.

Most everything else was good, or at least neutral. The government might tax and regulate, but traditionally it does not focus on protecting consumers from the consequences of overindulgence. The health department may regulate what goes into a doughnut, but not how many doughnuts go into you.

Reality is closer to a continuum. Alcohol, nicotine and caffeine are psychoactive chemicals that can cause varying degrees of problems, but they were never lumped together with heroin. And even when cannabis was prohibited, neither sentencing guidelines nor the public equated its dangers with crack. The public was sophisticated enough to know that some drugs cause more harm.

Gambling also challenges black-and-white thinking. It triggers neural pathways similar to those activated by drug addiction, and the American Psychiatric Association’s diagnostic manual recognizes that it can produce compulsive, self-destructive behavior even without a drug involved. Yet no compulsion-inducing product – not even the powerful synthetic opioid fentanyl – always induces addictive or self-destructive behavior. After all, many patients have “used” fentanyl during surgery.

Countries regulate gambling with that variation in mind. Until recent decades, the U.S. banned commercial sports betting . Japan limits casino visits to a set number per week or month. Norway permits gambling only via state monopolies aimed at preventing gambling problems and at funneling profits to nonprofits.

I’m not arguing that Japan’s or Norway’s gambling policies are right, or that the U.S. should follow Australia , Indonesia and Malaysia in blocking youth social media accounts. I’m only suggesting such actions merit real debate, not automatic dismissal.

Binary distinctions between bad and good don’t work because products and their features vary widely in how likely they are to cause regrettable, repetitive engagement. Free societies rightly presume that adults can manage their own affairs without government interference – but children are a different matter, and even adult freedom has exceptions.

Pennsylvania’s lawsuit charges that TikTok is engineered to trap users and thereby maximize the time they spend generating revenue for the company. That is reminiscent of cigarette manufacturers intentionally modifying chemical formulations , such as adding ammonia compounds , to enhance the speed and efficiency of nicotine absorption to maintain user addiction.

On the other hand, keeping users continuously engaged – through casino floor design, gym membership contracts or automated billing for subscriptions – is a mainstream strategy across industries. Plenty of legal, respected organizations use it to maximize profit.

Likewise, reputable studies also find some degree of dopamine response to video games , milkshakes and even music . The intensity of that response is far lower than what drugs such as cocaine or heroin produce, but it illustrates that one should not leap from the mere existence of a dopamine response to a reflexive ban.

Ideally, legislatures would strike a balance between freedom and protecting the minority who’d misuse it. But lately, state and national legislatures have been stalled by partisan division , swayed by commercial interests and reluctant to pass new restrictions .

Given this legislative lethargy, state attorneys general sometimes step in to protect the public from companies that exploit compulsion-inducing products. Pittsburgh Public Schools made a similar case years before Sunday’s lawsuit: The district sued TikTok and other social media platforms in federal court, arguing the companies induced students to “compulsively use their services” and left the district to absorb the resulting mental health costs. That case, consolidated with similar suits from districts nationwide , ended when TikTok settled rather than go to trial this spring – a resolution that came just months before Pennsylvania filed its own case making a similar addictive-by-design argument.

Important elements of modern tobacco control came not from Congress but from the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement . This agreement resolved lawsuits brought by state attorneys general against major cigarette manufacturers. It also eliminated cigarette billboard ads, cartoon mascots like Joe Camel, most free samples and tobacco-brand sponsorships, and it banned cigarette marketing aimed at youth. Congress didn’t give the FDA broad authority over tobacco until a decade later, in 2009.

The opioid crisis provides a more recent example. Settlements of lawsuits against opioid manufacturers, distributors and pharmacy chains imposed not only billion-dollar fines but also rules governing future conduct. Johnson & Johnson agreed to stop selling and promoting opioids for 10 years. Major drug distributors agreed to stronger systems for identifying suspicious wholesale opioid orders and sharing distribution data, while CVS, Walgreens and Walmart agreed to systems for flagging suspicious opioid prescriptions. Litigation accomplished some of the work ordinarily associated with regulation.

Regulation by litigation has drawbacks. Courts and attorneys general are no substitute for legislatures and expert regulatory agencies. But when conventional regulation fails to keep pace with powerful new products capable of inducing self-destructive, compulsive consumption, courts offer another route.

The path Attorney General Sunday has now opened may prove long and contentious, but the TikTok suit could come to be seen as the beginning of an important new layer of public protection against compulsion-inducing product design.

articles.title: A second hurricane just sideswiped Hawaii – why the islands’ usual force field seems to be down in 2026
articles.author:
<name>Nicholas Grondin, Assistant Professor of Environmental Studies, University of Tampa</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/nicholas-grondin-1047350"/>
paras: The Hawaiian Islands rarely see significant hurricane damage , but they just experienced the effects of their second hurricane in a year as Hurricane Lowell’s eyewall brushed Niihau, west of Kauai, on Sept. 8, 2026.

The hurricane brought heavy downpours, high surf and hurricane-force wind gusts that pounded both islands, knocking out power and flooding roads . Tropical storm conditions reached as far as Honolulu on the island of Oahu.

Lowell was the 14th named Pacific storm of 2026 and the fifth hurricane. The one that formed right after it, Hurricane Marie, sent big waves to Southern California , eroding coastal areas , and the Pacific hurricane season doesn’t end until Nov. 30. By some metrics, the season has had the most active start since 2021.
In August, a near-miss by Hurricane Lala brought hurricane-force winds to the Hawaii’s Big Island for the first time since 1871.

People joke that the Hawaiian Islands have a force field keeping hurricanes away. But this year, a few things are keeping that force field down. I’m one of the few atmospheric scientists whose research focuses on Pacific hurricanes . Here’s what I’m seeing in the eastern and central Pacific basins this year.

For decades, Hawaii was thought of as a special place that somehow dodged hurricanes despite its tropical location. While it lies at a similar latitude to other hurricane-prone regions, such as the Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico or the Bahamas, significant hurricane damage is rare there.
Hurricanes Dot (1959) , Iwa (1982) , Iniki (1992) and Lane (2018) were the most notable storms in the islands’ recorded history.
Iniki is often considered the worst: Its 145 mph wind gusts damaged about 70% of Kauai’s homes and businesses and more than 550 buildings on Oahu.
There are two reasons for Hawaii’s lack of more frequent hurricane impacts.

First, Hawaii is a pretty small target over the vast Pacific Ocean. The probability of a hurricane passing over any particular point is low, especially farther from the Mexican coast, since most Pacific hurricanes tend to stay closer to Mexico.

Second, the ocean itself forms a hurricane shield of sorts for the islands. The ocean has cooler water temperatures to the east , where most storms approaching the islands come from. Without warm oceans to provide fuel, hurricanes tend to weaken and fizzle out as they approach the islands.

Hawaii is often affected by weaker and decaying tropical systems, but their impacts are typically limited to localized flooding and large waves. That’s what Hawaii saw from Hurricane Kiko in 2025 as it weakened passing north of the islands.

In 2026, Lala also approached the islands from the east, but it stayed at a lower latitude, which allowed the storm to intensify over warmer-than-normal waters. Most of the storms that approach the islands from the east are forced to battle the normal “shield” of cooler ocean temperatures located to the east of the islands.

Lowell, like Dot, Iniki, and Lane, took a different journey this year. While all four of those storms developed to the east-southeast of the islands, they all tracked south of the islands before making a sharp turn toward the north or northwest to head toward Hawaii.
Dot and Iniki made landfall on Kauai , one of the westernmost islands. Iniki was the only known landfall of a major hurricane – a Category 3 storm or higher – in the state.

In 2018, Hurricane Lane turned toward Oahu, but it weakened due to increasingly hostile atmospheric conditions – including increased vertical wind shear , with faster winds near the top of the storm than the bottom, making it harder for the storm to keep its organized structure – and a drier, more stable air mass. While it didn’t make landfall, Lane still brought record-breaking rainfall to the islands, with as much as 58 inches (1.47 meters) falling on the Big Island.

In the eastern and central Pacific, the most common tropical storm track is a nearly straight line toward the west, driven by an atmospheric feature known as the Hawaiian High or subtropical ridge . This semipermanent high-pressure system sits to the northeast of Hawaii.

The Hawaiian High’s sinking air makes it harder for hurricanes to draw heat and moisture from the ocean. The result is pleasant conditions for the islands while hurricanes are steered around the edge of the high-pressure system.

The typical pattern around the high directs storms to the west, missing the islands. However, occasionally, low-pressure troughs can migrate southward and turn a storm toward the north, increasing its acceleration in the process, as happened with Lowell .
Another important player on the Pacific hurricane scene is El Niño.

During strong El Niño years, like 2026, the tropical Pacific is much warmer than normal. The ocean tends to be busier with hurricanes during El Niño, while the Atlantic is typically quieter – as we’re seeing in 2026.

Researchers at the University of Hawaii-Manoa identified a significant increase in the frequency and likelihood of tropical cyclones in the vicinity of Hawaii during El Niño years compared with other years. They hypothesize that El Niño years favor more Hawaiian systems due to increases in atmospheric humidity and favorable wind patterns in the region.

The most notable change during El Niño years is the warmer-than-normal ocean temperatures, particularly to the south and east of Hawaii. These warmer temperatures supported Lala intensifying into Category 1 hurricane as it approached the Big Island from the east and passed just south of the chain.

Multiple studies have also noted that increases in hurricane activity across the western portion of the eastern Pacific and the central Pacific generally are seen during El Niño years as well, such as in 2015 .
Generally, as the season progresses into fall, hurricanes near Hawaii become less likely, while the risk of hurricane landfalls rises for the Pacific coast of Mexico .
In recent years, several powerful Pacific storms have made landfall in Mexico, including Hurricanes Willa (2018) , Roslyn (2022) and Otis (2023) , all of which hit during the last third of October.
The Atlantic, meanwhile, is forecast to remain much less active than normal , even through the peak months of its 2026 hurricane season.

articles.title: ‘Fountain’ might make you laugh or scowl but asks important questions – a Philly art historian explains why Marcel Duchamp’s iconic 1917 sculpture still provokes
articles.author:
<name>Matthew Palczynski, Adjunct Faculty, Art History, Temple University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/matthew-palczynski-2751205"/>
paras: Marcel Duchamp’s “Fountain” is not for everyone – and it does not need to be.
But it does encapsulate a central concern in the philosophy of art: What makes something art, and who gets to decide?
Whatever our tastes, art can challenge accepted systems and make us reconsider what we think we know.
Duchamp’s friend and chess partner John Cage observed in 1988 , “I can’t understand why people are frightened of new ideas. I’m frightened of the old ones.” “Fountain” embodies this thinking.

A version of “Fountain” is part of the Philadelphia Museum of Art’s permanent collection and will appear in the museum’s upcoming Duchamp retrospective , which opens Oct. 10, 2026, and runs through Jan. 31, 2027. The exhibition will revisit Duchamp’s enduring questions about what art is and what it can be.

As an art historian and former Philadelphia Museum of Art staff lecturer, I have developed an intimate knowledge of Duchamp’s art through years of teaching his work. During and after my tenure at the museum, I presented 101 lectures and led 25 gallery-based programs. Some of these focused directly on Duchamp, while others explored broader questions about originality, authorship, intention, skill and value.
These questions are embedded in the remarkable story of “Fountain.”
The 1917 original “Fountain” survives only in photographs, but 14 authorized full-scale replicas followed. The Philadelphia Museum of Art owns the earliest, signed by Duchamp in 1950.

“Fountain” continued a press narrative about Duchamp’s work that had begun four years earlier when his 1912 painting “ Nude Descending a Staircase (No. 2) ” became a sensation at the 1913 Armory Show in New York City. Journalist Julian Street remarked that it resembled “ the explosion of a shingle factory .”
Former president Theodore Roosevelt declared that a Navajo rug in his bathroom was “ a far more satisfactory and decorative picture ” than the cubist artists on display at the armory.
By 1917, Duchamp knew that controversy could compel audiences to debate what qualified as art. With “Fountain” that debate became part of the artwork.

Its story began with the Society of Independent Artists exhibition in New York in April 1917. Duchamp had helped found the society and establish its democratic premise that every member could exhibit without a jury. He tested that principle by purchasing a porcelain urinal, turning it on its side, signing it “R. Mutt 1917” and submitting it under a pseudonym.

The organizers excluded it from the official display and placed it behind a partition outside the main exhibition area. Collector Walter Arensberg, Duchamp’s friend and fellow board member, defended it and reportedly intended to purchase it . Both men resigned in protest.

Alfred Stieglitz photographed “Fountain” at his 291 gallery positioned in front of Marsden Hartley’s 1913 painting “ The Warriors .” The painting depicts a German military parade, and the title of the painting suggests a battle between old and new ways of thinking. Stieglitz’s photograph appeared in the May 1917 issue of The Blind Man , a short-lived New York avant-garde art magazine, alongside an editorial that argued that Duchamp’s act of choosing an ordinary object created “a new thought for that object.”

Duchamp called such objects “readymades,” a term historians believe he first used in a letter to his sister Suzanne dated Jan. 15, 1916. His first so-called readymade was “Bicycle Wheel” (1913), which joined an inverted bicycle wheel to a wooden stool. The lost original survives through replicas, including an authorized version from 1964 that’s held at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
“Bicycle Wheel” proposed that art doesn’t have to be handmade. An object can become art because the artist selects it and invites us to think about it differently.

Duchamp studied at the Académie Julian in Paris and was fully capable of traditional drawing and painting. He arrived at the readymades not because he lacked technical ability, but because he prioritized art that engaged the mind over what he called “ retinal art ,” art that primarily pleased the eye.

Seeing “Fountain” in Philadelphia provides a key to two of the museum’s other great Duchamp works: “ The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even (The Large Glass) ” and “ Étant donnés .” The eroticism that “Fountain” implied with its associations to bodily functions evolved into frustrated desire in “The Large Glass.” In “Étant donnés,” the eroticism becomes explicit and voyeuristic, as it asks viewers to peer through holes in a weathered door.

Duchamp’s nod to manufactured plumbing systems in “Fountain” also anticipates his exploration of mechanical themes. In “The Large Glass,” the nine bachelors form part of an elaborate mechanical apparatus . In “Étant donnés,” an electric motor inside a cookie tin rotates a perforated disc, creating the illusion of a moving waterfall.

All three works shift art away from a self-contained image and toward an encounter involving object, idea, context, chance and viewer. “Fountain” transforms plumbing through the artist’s selection. “The Large Glass” incorporates chance through cracks created when it was shattered accidentally in transit – damage Duchamp repaired and embraced. “Étant donnés” incorporates found materials, including an old wooden door Duchamp obtained in Cadaqués, the Catalonian village where he and his wife, Alexina “Teeny” Duchamp, spent their summers.

Together, the works demonstrate that art can be a question to contemplate, a system to decipher, or an experience our actions complete. Seen together in Philadelphia, they reveal how consistently Duchamp made the viewer central to artistic meaning.

Despite its philosophical seriousness, “Fountain” is deliberately absurd and comical. It is appropriate to laugh. I’ve seen viewers even get angry and irritated. Its irreverent humor, provocation and rejection of artistic convention place it within Dada, a movement that began at Zurich’s Cabaret Voltaire in 1916 as an absurdist protest against the nationalism and supposedly rational values that had led to World War I. Dada became an international movement active in Berlin, Paris and New York, and it transformed modern art.

The legacy of the readymades, especially “Fountain,” is difficult to overstate. They paved the way for Louise Nevelson, who transformed discarded pieces of wood into monumental assemblages , and Andy Warhol, who elevated Campbell’s soup cans into icons of American culture. Maurizio Cattelan addressed Fountain directly in 2016 with “ America ,” a fully functioning toilet cast in 18-karat gold.

Nearly a century later, Cattelan echoed Duchamp’s questions about where artistic value resides: Is it in the object, its material, its price, its context, the artist’s idea or the institution declaring it art?
This leads to the great paradox of Duchamp’s legacy. Art conceived to challenge permanence, originality and inherent value has itself become permanent, invaluable and iconic.

articles.title: The Women’s Professional Baseball League is betting that women’s baseball has a future in the US
articles.author:
<name>Callie Maddox, Associate Professor of Sport Leadership and Management, Miami University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/callie-maddox-2349208"/>
paras: Over 70 years after the dissolution of the All-American Professional Girls’ Baseball League – and nearly 30 years since the end of the short-lived Ladies League Baseball – female baseball players have been competing in a professional league of their own.

The Women’s Professional Baseball League began its inaugural season on Aug. 1, 2026, in front of a sellout crowd at Robin Roberts Stadium in Springfield, Illinois. Since then, the league’s four teams have battled one another across 30 games, producing highlight reel moments like Kelsie Whitmore’s three-homer game and Andréanne Leblanc’s walk-off grand slam .
The San Francisco Firebells finished the regular season atop the standings . The playoffs, beginning on Sept. 9, will determine the league champion.
The WPBL is appearing at a time when women’s sports in the U.S. are thriving.

Established leagues such as the WNBA and National Women’s Soccer League are seeing more investment, higher team valuations, lucrative media deals and growing fanbases. Women’s sports revenue is projected to reach roughly US$3 billion in 2026 – an increase of 340% in just four years.

The WPBL certainly hopes to capitalize on this moment. But the league is also doing something culturally significant: providing a pathway for the thousands of girls and women who choose to play baseball, not softball .

In the U.S., women have been playing baseball since at least the 1860s. But stubborn stereotypes continue to cast baseball as a sport for men and softball as the acceptable equivalent for women. Following legal challenges, Little League Baseball officially allowed girls to play in 1974. However, that same year, Little League Softball was founded, which steered girls away from baseball and reinforced the gendered split of the two sports.

Since then, there have been limited opportunities and resources available to girls and women in the U.S. who want to play baseball. Those who play Little League Baseball almost always switch to softball by high school. At the collegiate level, there are a handful of women’s baseball club teams , but it is not an NCAA-sanctioned sport.

Female ballplayers in other countries also face some of these issues. But I’ve researched and written about how developmental pipelines for women’s baseball players in Japan, Canada and Australia are far more established than they are in the U.S.

So it’s no surprise that nearly half of the 65 players in the Women’s Professional Baseball League hail from other countries, including 11 from Canada, eight from Japan, five from Mexico and four from Australia.

Japan’s Ayami Sato , picked second in the draft, is widely considered the best women’s baseball pitcher in the world. Thaima Maximiliana , from Curacao, was a first-round draft pick for Los Angeles, and South Korea’s Hyeonah Kim signed with Boston as the fourth overall pick.
That said, many of the American ballplayers had already made a name for themselves prior to joining the WBPL.

Kelsie Whitmore , who plays for the Savannah Bananas , a traveling team known for its entertaining style of play, was the league’s first overall pick. The Bananas play Banana Ball , a fast-paced variation of baseball with unconventional rules that puts spectacle and fan engagement at the heart of the game. Other women in Banana Ball to sign with the WPBL include Denae Benites , Val Perez , Ashton Lansdell and Mo’ne Davis , who became the first girl to pitch a shutout at the Little League World Series in 2014. Davis actually scored the WPBL’s first run .
The league also features women who play for the USA Baseball women’s national team , which recently qualified for next year’s Women’s Baseball World Cup.

Each WPBL team has a salary cap of US$95,000, so players will earn roughly $6,333 for the short, eight-week season. The league is covering housing costs and living expenses for the players, and they also receive a share of the league’s sponsorship revenue, in addition to any personal endorsement deals they might secure.
Even though the teams hail from other cities, all of the games for the inaugural season have taken place in Springfield, Illinois.
The location is symbolic: Springfield is where the first ticketed baseball game between two women’s teams, the Blondes and the Brunettes , took place in 1875.

In similar spirit, the team names commemorate trailblazing women. The New York Heights are named after civil rights leader Dorothy Height . The Boston Hunters pay tribute to Harriot K. Hunt , an influential medical doctor and women’s rights activist. The San Francisco Firebells honor Lillie Hitchcock Coit , a philanthropist and patron of the city’s volunteer firefighters whose nickname was “Firebelle Lil.” And the Los Angeles Queens are named after Lizzie Murphy, known as the “ Queen of Baseball .” Murphy was the first woman to play against Major League Baseball players when she faced Boston Red Sox players in an exhibition game at Fenway Park in 1922.

Meanwhile, the official league mascot is one of the most unique in professional sports: a dancing, cartwheeling version of Maybelle Blair , the 99-year-old former All-American Professional Girls’ Baseball League player.
ESPN Select has been broadcasting the entire season for the U.S. market, with select games also being shown on the Scripps Sports Network. Fans outside of the U.S. must tune in via YouTube.
Even though the regular season only included 30 games, there was plenty of drama on and off the field.

The manager of the Boston Hunters, former MLB All-Star closer Keith Foulke , was fired just three games into the season. Three weeks later, the league faced scrutiny after a board member filed a civil complaint alleging misuse of funds and conflicts of interest in the board’s makeup and hiring practices.

Yet play continued and proved exciting. San Francisco claimed the league’s first walk-off win in a game that featured two grand slams. New York’s Jaida Lee emerged as a top pitcher and led the league in strikeouts and strikeout rate. Whitmore and Benites finished the season leading the league with 11 home runs apiece .

Despite the success of its inaugural season, the WPBL is ultimately a startup that faces the challenges of any new league: It needs to grow its fan base, boost its media coverage, provide quality broadcasting and remain financially solvent.
So what will it take for the WPBL to survive, expand and carve out its own identity in an increasingly saturated pro sports landscape?

It’s worth looking to other emerging sports and leagues. Flag football is growing thanks to its inclusion as an Olympic sport and promotional and financial support from the NFL. Both Women’s Elite Rugby and the Women’s Lacrosse League hope to leverage increased interest and investment to succeed. And the Athletes United Softball League is utilizing its innovative rules to engage fans.
Questions linger about the future of the WPBL. But the league certainly has one thing in its favor: the rich history of women playing baseball, both in the U.S. and around the world.
